cards.title: Load Balancing (L4 vs L7, Health Checks, Algorithms)
cards.question: Explain Load Balancing (L4 vs L7, Health Checks, Algorithms)
cards.answer_30s: L4 load balancers route TCP/UDP packets using IP/port without inspecting payloads (ultra-fast). L7 load balancers terminate TLS and inspect HTTP headers, cookies, and URLs for smart routing. Algorithms include Round Robin, Least Connections, and Consistent Hashing.

code.body: # L7: path routing (/api -> API pool, /static -> CDN), TLS termination, rate limiting

cards.typical_use: Distributing traffic across stateless app tiers with zero-downtime health checks.
pitfalls: Mention active vs passive health checks and graceful connection draining.

cards.title: CAP & PACELC Theorems
cards.question: Explain CAP & PACELC Theorems
cards.answer_30s: CAP states a distributed store under a Network Partition (P) must choose Consistency (CP: linearizable reads, may reject writes) or Availability (AP: always responds, may serve stale data). PACELC extends CAP: even Else (no partition), systems trade off Latency (L) vs Consistency (C).

code.body: # CP: ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase | AP: DynamoDB (default), Cassandra | CA doesn't exist in distributed networks

cards.typical_use: Justifying database choices in distributed system designs.
pitfalls: Bringing up PACELC shows deeper systems maturity than CAP alone.

cards.title: Consistent Hashing & Virtual Nodes
cards.question: Explain Consistent Hashing & Virtual Nodes
cards.answer_30s: Modulo hashing (`hash(key) % N`) remaps nearly all keys when a cache/shard node is added or removed. Consistent hashing maps nodes and keys onto a 0..2^32-1 ring so adding/removing a node only moves ~1/N keys. Virtual nodes prevent uneven load distribution.

code.body: # Virtual nodes (e.g. 150 vnodes per physical server) smooth hot spots on the hash ring

cards.typical_use: Partitioning distributed caches (Redis/Memcached) and NoSQL shards.
pitfalls: Explain how consistent hashing minimizes cache misses during autoscaling.

cards.title: Multi-Tier Caching & CDN Strategies
cards.question: Explain Multi-Tier Caching & CDN Strategies
cards.answer_30s: Layer caches from edge to storage: Browser Cache-Control -> CDN Edge -> API Gateway/L1 In-Memory -> Distributed L2 (Redis) -> DB Buffer Pool. Use Cache-Aside for general reads, Write-Through for consistency, and Randomized TTLs + Singleflight to prevent stampedes.
cards.typical_use: Scaling read-heavy systems from 1k to 100k+ QPS.
pitfalls: Always quantify cache hit ratio impact on DB QPS during back-of-the-envelope math.

cards.title: Database Scaling: Read Replicas, Partitioning & Sharding
cards.question: Explain Database Scaling: Read Replicas, Partitioning & Sharding
cards.answer_30s: Scale reads with Read Replicas; scale single-node tables with vertical scaling + Partitioning; scale writes horizontally with Sharding (hash, range, or directory-based). Sharding introduces cross-shard join/transaction complexity and hot-shard risks—delay sharding until truly needed.

code.body: # Shard key choice is critical: shard by tenant_id or user_id to keep user queries on 1 shard

pitfalls: Always address cross-shard queries, resharding pain, and replication lag.

cards.title: Rate Limiting Algorithms (Token Bucket, Sliding Window)
cards.question: Explain Rate Limiting Algorithms (Token Bucket, Sliding Window)
cards.answer_30s: Rate limiters protect APIs from abuse and cascading overload. Token Bucket allows controlled bursts; Leaky Bucket smooths output rate; Fixed Window has boundary spikes; Sliding Window Log/Counter (in Redis) gives accurate rolling limits.

code.body: # Distributed Token Bucket via atomic Redis Lua script keyed by user_id / IP

cards.typical_use: Protecting login, AI inference, and public APIs.
pitfalls: Return `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers.

cards.title: Idempotency Keys & Retries with Backoff + Jitter
cards.question: Explain Idempotency Keys & Retries with Backoff + Jitter
cards.answer_30s: Networks fail ambiguously; retries can cause duplicate payments or orders. Clients send a unique `Idempotency-Key` header stored atomically by the server so retries return the original result. Always pair retries with exponential backoff AND jitter to prevent thundering herds.
cards.typical_use: Payment gateways, webhook consumers, and resilient microservice RPCs.
pitfalls: Combine Idempotency-Key with a DB unique constraint for ironclad protection.

cards.title: Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads & Backpressure
cards.question: Explain Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads & Backpressure
cards.answer_30s: A Circuit Breaker (Closed -> Open -> Half-Open) fails fast when a downstream service is degraded, preventing thread-pool exhaustion. Bulkheads isolate resources per dependency; Backpressure (bounded queues, 429/503) stops producers from overwhelming consumers.

code.body: # Closed (normal) -> Open (fail fast for 30s) -> Half-Open (probe 1-3 requests)

cards.typical_use: Preventing single-service brownouts from cascading across the whole platform.
pitfalls: Mention adaptive concurrency limits and load shedding as advanced resilience tools.

cards.title: Distributed Transactions: 2PC vs Saga Pattern
cards.question: Explain Distributed Transactions: 2PC vs Saga Pattern
cards.answer_30s: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) blocks locks across services and hurts availability at scale. The Saga pattern breaks a distributed workflow into local transactions paired with compensating actions on failure (via Choreography events or Orchestration state machines like Temporal).

code.body: # Order Saga: Reserve Inventory -> Charge Card -> (if fail: Release Inventory)

cards.typical_use: Managing cross-service workflows in e-commerce and travel booking.
pitfalls: Highlight that Saga provides eventual consistency (ACD, not full isolation), so design for semantic locks/pending states.

cards.title: Q: How do you approach a System Design interview in 45 minutes?
cards.question: Q: How do you approach a System Design interview in 45 minutes?
cards.answer_30s: A: 1) Clarify functional & non-functional requirements (scale, QPS, latency, consistency) in 5 mins. 2) Back-of-the-envelope capacity math (storage, bandwidth, QPS). 3) High-level API & architecture diagram. 4) Deep dive into bottlenecks, data model, caching, partitioning, and failure modes. 5) Observability & trade-offs.

code.body: # Always drive the conversation and verify requirements before drawing boxes

cards.typical_use: Meta-framework for acing any system design round.
pitfalls: Never jump straight into Kubernetes/Kafka without justifying WHY the scale requires them.

cards.title: Q: Design a URL Shortener (e.g. TinyURL) — key decisions?
cards.question: Q: Design a URL Shortener (e.g. TinyURL) — key decisions?
cards.answer_30s: A: Read-heavy (100:1). Generate 7-char Base62 IDs from distributed counters (Snowflake/ZooKeeper ranges) or hash+collision check (no collisions with pre-allocated counter ranges). Store in KV/NoSQL or sharded SQL, cache hot URLs in Redis, return 301 (browser-cached, lower server load) vs 302 (tracks analytics).
pitfalls: 301 vs 302 redirect trade-off is almost always asked as a follow-up.

cards.title: Q: Push (Fan-out on Write) vs Pull (Fan-out on Read) for a Social Feed?
cards.question: Q: Push (Fan-out on Write) vs Pull (Fan-out on Read) for a Social Feed?
cards.answer_30s: A: Fan-out on Write pushes new posts to followers' precomputed feed caches (O(1) fast reads, expensive for celebrities with 10M followers). Fan-out on Read queries followed users' posts at read time (cheap writes, slower reads). Use a Hybrid: push for normal users, pull/merge at read time for celebrities.

code.body: # Hybrid Fan-out: Fan-out on write (<10k followers) + Fan-out on read (celebrities)

pitfalls: The Hybrid approach is the canonical expected answer.

cards.title: Q: WebSockets vs SSE vs Long Polling — how do you choose for real-time updates?
cards.question: Q: WebSockets vs SSE vs Long Polling — how do you choose for real-time updates?
cards.answer_30s: A: Long Polling is simple HTTP fallback (higher overhead). Server-Sent Events (SSE) provide lightweight unidirectional server-to-client streaming over HTTP with auto-reconnect (great for AI streaming, notifications, live feeds). WebSockets provide full-duplex bidirectional low-latency TCP (chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing).

code.body: # AI token streaming & notifications -> SSE | Chat & gaming -> WebSockets

pitfalls: Explain how stateful WebSocket servers scale behind L7 load balancers using Redis Pub/Sub for cross-pod message routing.

cards.title: Q: How do you generate unique, sortable distributed IDs without a single DB bottleneck?
cards.question: Q: How do you generate unique, sortable distributed IDs without a single DB bottleneck?
cards.answer_30s: A: Use 64-bit Snowflake IDs (41 bits timestamp + 10 bits machine/datacenter ID + 12 bits per-ms sequence) for time-ordered, index-friendly IDs at millions/sec with zero coordination, or UUIDv7 (time-ordered) instead of random UUIDv4 which causes B-Tree page fragmentation.

code.body: # UUIDv7 / Snowflake > UUIDv4 for B-Tree primary key insert performance

pitfalls: Pointing out that random UUIDv4 fragments B-Tree indexes while UUIDv7/Snowflake keeps inserts sequential is a great senior insight.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between Availability and Reliability, and SLA vs SLO vs SLI?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between Availability and Reliability, and SLA vs SLO vs SLI?
cards.answer_30s: A: SLI is the measured metric (e.g. p99 latency < 200ms). SLO is the internal target (99.9% of requests meet SLI over 30 days, leaving a 0.1% error budget). SLA is the external customer contract with penalties. Availability is uptime; Reliability is performing correctly without data loss or corruption.
pitfalls: Explain error budgets: when budget is healthy, ship features fast; when exhausted, freeze features and fix reliability.

cards.title: Q: How do you design a distributed Notification / Webhook delivery system?
cards.question: Q: How do you design a distributed Notification / Webhook delivery system?
cards.answer_30s: A: Decouple ingestion behind an API + SQS/Kafka partitioned by tenant. Workers deliver with strict per-endpoint timeouts, exponential backoff + jitter, circuit breakers for dead customer endpoints, HMAC-SHA256 payload signatures for authenticity, and DLQs + delivery logs for debugging.
cards.typical_use: Common practical backend system design prompt.
pitfalls: Mention noisy-neighbor isolation: one slow customer webhook must not starve delivery queues for other customers.
